title: Where a New Sitepackage Comes From
hints: Nothing in the core creates a sitepackage, and three community tools divide the work. The Site Package Builder at get.typo3.org is a web form that hands the extension back as a download. The console tool is the extension friendsoftypo3/kickstarter, which writes single parts of a sitepackage into an export directory of its own and asks before it replaces what stands there. b13/make writes neither a site package nor an Extbase extension and says so, so it answers the rest of an extension instead.

The builder answers a request as well as the form: a POST of JSON to its sitepackage endpoint returns the extension as a zip. Fetch https://get.typo3.org/api/doc.json before you build the request, and take the endpoint, the fields and the values each one accepts from there rather than from an example. A value the builder refuses comes back as a Bad Request that names the field.

The builder derives the Composer vendor and the PHP namespace from author.company, and the package name and the extension key from title. So a request sets those two fields to the vendor and the name the package is meant to carry.

hints.text: The builder writes its own tree, and each part has a place in the one the sitepackage-layout hint gives. Resources/Private/PageView/Pages and its Layouts and Partials go below Resources/Private/Templates/, the layout into Layouts/Pages/. Resources/Private/ContentElements/ goes to the content element subdirectories of the same root, and Configuration/Sets/<Set>/PageTsConfig/BackendLayouts/ to the set's BackendLayouts/. Its settings.yaml sets values for constants that no settings.definitions.yaml declares.

The set is the half the console covers: make:site-set writes Configuration/Sets/<Set>/config.yaml and prints the dependencies line the site configuration needs, and make:site-settings-definition writes the definitions beside it. make:site-package refuses here and names the reason, so the extension around that set comes from the builder, or from the layout theme_camino works out.
make:site-package is the console form of the builder: it asks what the web form asks and fetches the result from get.typo3.org, so nothing is downloaded by hand.

hints: A generated sitepackage is a starting point rather than a layout to keep, and the builder's own documentation says it writes a large number of unnecessary, mostly empty files. What each directory in it is for is the sitepackage-layout hint.

title: How a Sitepackage Is Laid Out

hints.text: The core ships a theme of its own — the package typo3/theme-camino, typo3/sysext/theme_camino in a core checkout, absent from a Composer project that did not require it. It is where the layout below is worked out in full, so read it rather than invent one. Read, not depend on: it is the theme of one release line, announced to move out of the core into a repository of its own, and a project sitepackage that requires it or extends its set buys that migration for nothing.

The language files are split by who reads them — the frontend messages, the backend field labels, the backend layout titles, the content element previews. Each file is its own translation domain, and the domain is what a label is referenced by, so the split is what makes the references readable.

hints: All of this is the extension. What sits around it in a project — where the browser tests go, what belongs in Build/, which scripts the repository exposes — is its own subject, because the core has no answer for it: it is not a project. That is the project repository layout hint.

hints.text: Where the project does not have theme_camino, the tree is this. Configuration/Sets/<Set>/ holds config.yaml, settings.yaml where the set defines settings, setup.typoscript, page.tsconfig, TypoScript/ and BackendLayouts/. Resources/Private/Templates/ holds Pages/, Content/, Layouts/Pages/, Layouts/Content/ and Partials/. Resources/Private/Language/ holds the language files, and Resources/Public/ the CSS, the JavaScript and the icons.

hints: Where the files themselves go is its own hint: sitepackage-templates for the template root, sitepackage-backend-layouts for the page layouts, sitepackage-typoscript-reference for how one object reaches another.

title: The Fluid Template Root and What Is Addressed From It

hints.text: A template file ends in .fluid.html, and Fluid reads a plain .html as well.
A template file ends in .html. This Fluid does not read .fluid.html, so a file named that way is not found.

hints: One template root carries all of it: Resources/Private/Templates/, with Pages/ for the page templates, Content/ for the content element templates, ContentPreviews/ for their backend previews, Layouts/, and Partials/ grouped in subdirectories. That directory is the single paths entry PAGEVIEW is given, and lib.contentElement is pointed at Templates/Content/ with the same Layouts/ and Partials/ — so the page and its content elements are rendered out of one tree instead of two.

A layout is addressed with its subdirectory: <f:layout name="Pages/Default" /> in a page template, <f:layout name="Content/Default" /> in a content element. The page frame and the content element frame are both called Default, and fluid_styled_content ships a Default of its own, so a shared Layouts/ root without those subdirectories renders the site header and footer inside every single content element — on a page that still comes back without an error.

The partial root is the same shared name space, and the collision there is not confined to the element that causes it: fluid_styled_content ships Partials/Header/Header and renders it from Partials/Header/All, so a partial of that name in a later root renders the header of every core element on the page. It is handed the core's arguments rather than its own, so a required argument the core does not pass turns every page carrying a core element into an exception, where the layout collision rendered the wrong thing without one. Footer/, Media/, Bullets/, Table/ and DropIn/ sit beside it in that root, so an extension adding partialRootPaths to lib.contentElement puts its own partials under a directory name nothing else uses.

Both collisions concern the roots of lib.contentElement and PAGEVIEW and nothing else. An Extbase plugin renders from roots of its own, and plugin-template-override says how a sitepackage overrides those.

A content element names its own template: fluid_styled_content sets templateName = Default on lib.contentElement and ships no Default template, and every element it renders sets its own beside its rendering definition — Configuration/TypoScript/ContentElement/Text.typoscript is tt_content.text =< lib.contentElement followed by templateName = Text. An element copied off lib.contentElement without one carries Default and asks for a template neither package ships.

hints.text: Deriving the name from the CType instead is theme_camino's configuration, and a sitepackage inherits that convention only by reproducing it: Configuration/Sets/camino/TypoScript/content.typoscript unsets templateName and sets templateName.ifEmpty.cObject on the CType field with case = uppercamelcase, so camino_textmedia_teaser renders Content/CaminoTextmediaTeaser.fluid.html. The same file points tt_content.default at lib.contentElement, so the derivation answers for every CType instead of for the ones a rendering definition names. Under it a snake_case CType is a requirement rather than a habit — words the identifier does not separate the file name does not separate either.

title: Where a Page Layout Is Declared
appliesTo: template name of a page layout
hints: One page layout per file, and one name for it: the identifier the file declares below mod.web_layout.BackendLayouts is also what the page template is named after, so the file name, the identifier and the page template Pages/<Name> are one name written in three places.

hints.text: Where those files live follows from one question — does anything reach a backend without the set? A project sitepackage ships one set and no Configuration/page.tsconfig of its own, so nothing does: the layouts belong in Configuration/Sets/<Set>/BackendLayouts/, pulled in with @import './BackendLayouts/*.tsconfig' from the set's page.tsconfig, which is the same place and the same form the TypoScript split already has. Configuration/BackendLayouts/ at extension level is for the other case — several sets, or a distributable theme like theme_camino, where the extension is the unit and an extension-level page.tsconfig carries what has to apply whether a site depends on the set or not. Where the extension has no such file, moving the layouts up there is an indirection with no effect. The directory keeps its name either way, because the name says what is in it: page TSconfig that is not a backend layout goes into page.tsconfig or a sibling directory, not in there.

A page with no layout selected takes the backend_layout_next_level of the nearest page above it, and the core's default layout where no page sets one. That layout has one column, colPos 0, with the identifier main. PAGEVIEW renders it with Pages/Default, so that template addresses content.main and no other area. A layout of the sitepackage's own named default shares that template with every page that selected nothing.

hints: An identifier must not contain two underscores in a row: the backend refuses it, because the pagets__ prefix is split off there to find the page template.

hints.text: PAGEVIEW takes the identifier without its pagets__ prefix as the template name below Pages/. Where no file carries that name exactly, it takes the same name with its first letter upper-cased. Nothing else in the name changes, so two_columns asks for Pages/Two_columns, and twoColumns for Pages/TwoColumns.

hints: A page layout file declares mod.web_layout.BackendLayouts.<identifier> with a title, an optional icon, and config.backend_layout. That block carries colCount, rowCount and rows.<n>.columns.<n>, and each column a name, a colPos, an identifier for the content area, and a colspan where it is wider than one. The title and every column name are LLL references into a language file the extension ships, and a key that file lacks shows as the raw reference in the page module.

hints.text: A page layout of the sitepackage's own named default stands beside the core's default rather than replacing it. The editor selects the sitepackage's one, and a page with nothing selected gets the core's one. Both render through Pages/Default, so that template works with the core's single area main as well as with the areas of the sitepackage's default.

hints: A page layout's icon becomes the icon of its entry in the page properties' layout field, so it takes what such an entry takes: an EXT: path to an image, or the identifier of a registered icon, which typo3_icon_lookup confirms.

title: Referencing a TypoScript Object Instead of Copying It
hints: An object reached with =< is a reference and not a copy: it is resolved while the page renders, out of the merged setup, so a data processor added to it in a file that is imported later still arrives. The copy operator < is the one where the order of the imports decides what the object ends up holding.
lib.contentElement is fluid_styled_content's object, so a sitepackage that depends on that extension reaches it with tt_content.<CType> =< lib.contentElement.

hints.text: lib.fluidPage is theme_camino's object: the camino set defines lib.fluidPage = PAGEVIEW and renders page.<n> =< lib.fluidPage. A sitepackage that does not depend on that set has no lib.fluidPage, and a reference to it renders nothing. It writes page.<n> = PAGEVIEW itself, or defines its own lib object before it references one.

title: What a Sitepackage Takes From fluid_styled_content
hints: The object a sitepackage takes the dependency for is lib.contentElement: a FLUIDTEMPLATE with templateName Default, the extension's own Templates, Partials and Layouts first and the styles.templates.* constants above them, and the settings the shipped templates read — the header type, the image lazy loading and decoding, the lightbox wrap. An element written as tt_content.<CType> =< lib.contentElement copies all of that and then overrides the template name.

hints.text: It also carries a dataProcessing entry of its own, record-transformation, so an element copying it is handed the transformed record rather than the raw row.

hints: lib.parseFunc and lib.parseFunc_RTE are not its. EXT:frontend declares both in its own ext_localconf.php, so rich text rendering is there whether or not this extension is required.

The typo3/fluid-styled-content-css set adds one thing: plugin.tx_frontend._CSS_DEFAULT_STYLE with the .ce-* rules that style the elements this extension renders. A site whose page TSconfig removes every one of those elements from the selector is shipping stylesheet rules for markup it never emits.

Defining lib.contentElement in the sitepackage instead is a FLUIDTEMPLATE of a few lines and drops the dependency, and what goes with it is the rendering of the core's own elements — text, textmedia, header, table, the menus. That is the decision to make deliberately: a site that keeps a few of them keeps the dependency, and one that offers only its own elements is paying for a scaffold it overrode.

Every Extbase plugin renders through this extension as well. ExtensionUtility::configurePlugin() writes tt_content.<plugin signature> =< lib.contentElement with templateName = Generic, and Generic is one of the templates this extension ships: it renders {content} where the plugin assigned it and otherwise an f:cObject back onto the plugin's own tt_content path, which is where the same call put the EXTBASEPLUGIN. EXT:form, EXT:felogin and EXT:indexed_search each register a plugin that way.

Dropping the dependency without putting lib.contentElement back leaves every one of those plugins silent. tt_content is a CASE on the CType and the plugin's own key is still written, so the yellow "has no rendering definition" default never fires and the element renders as nothing. Putting lib.contentElement back without a Generic template beside it fails the other way, with InvalidTemplateResourceException out of FLUIDTEMPLATE naming the template it looked for and every root it checked.

hints.text: A plugin registered with the list subtype takes a second path through this extension: tt_content.list is one of its content element files and sets templateName = List.

hints: The core's own elements are split across three extensions, and only the last part is this one's. EXT:frontend registers the CType and its TCA, EXT:backend draws the page module preview in StandardContentPreviewRenderer, and this extension holds the frontend rendering — Configuration/TypoScript/ContentElement/<Name>.typoscript and the template beside it. So dropping it leaves every core element still selectable and still previewed, and empty on the page. shortcut is the one to check first, because a site offering only its own elements tends to keep that one.

The Default layout renders Before, Header, Footer and After as optional sections whose fallback child is a partial — DropIn/Before/All, Header/All, Footer/All and DropIn/After/All. An element declaring none of those sections still renders those partials, so a layout written to replace this one owes the partials too or drops the sections deliberately.

The styles.templates.* and styles.content.* settings the shipped objects read are declared by this extension and by no other. A constant nothing declares is left as its own text — ConstantAwareTokenStream::__toString() falls back to the token — so a reference surviving the removal puts the literal {$styles...} into the value instead of emptying it.

title: Contrast and Visible Keyboard Focus on a Site Design
hints: A visible focus is a condition, not a selector. The WCAG non-text contrast criterion, level AA, asks the focus indicator for 3:1 against the colours adjacent to it.
So a :focus-visible rule satisfies nothing where its outline colour is close to the surface it lands on. Never remove an outline without an equal or better indicator in its place.

One focus colour cannot reach 3:1 against a light surface and a dark one at once. Declare it as a custom property and redefine it on each dark component, so the one :focus-visible rule takes the right value wherever it lands.

This ratio is computed rather than observed. The focus colour and every surface are declared values, so the WCAG relative luminance formula gives each ratio from two hex values before any browser runs.
Check it against every surface a link or a control sits on: the navigation, the header, the hero, the footer. browser-test-accessibility is the scan of the rendered page after it.
